text:
The chair had been put out on Delancey Street sometime before I noticed it, which is how things on the street usually go. It sat at the curb between a recycling bin and a dead ficus, an armchair with wooden arms and a barrel back. Fire had gotten to it, though not all of it. The left side was black and crackled like the skin of something roasted, while the right side remained a mild, defeated green. Someone had set it carefully upright, facing the road, as if it were waiting for a bus. I looked at it longer than was reasonable. Then it began to rain again, and I went on to the pharmacy.

It had been raining for nine days. People moved along the sidewalks with their shoulders raised, like men carrying invisible planks.

On my way back, under the awning of the shuttered dry cleaner's, I saw the couple. He was fiftyish, in a tan raincoat, with the faintly apologetic stoop of tall men. She was a little younger, or perhaps older, in a gray coat buttoned to the throat, carrying a paper bag of groceries against her chest, a leek poking out like a green flag. They were not touching. At the corner they stopped for the light, although there was no traffic, and waited with a patience I found almost unbearable.

I decided to follow them. I had never done such a thing; I am a person who returns library books early. But standing there with my little bag of cough drops, I felt I was being shown something, and that it would be rude to look away.

They turned down Marrow Street, which slopes toward the river, and I kept half a block behind. The gutters ran full, brown and fast, carrying leaves and cigarette filters and one small yellow sponge. The woman shifted the grocery bag from one arm to the other, and I saw how she held herself: her weight on the right side, the left shoulder turned slightly away, as though protecting it from a draft or a memory.

Their house was the fourth from the end, a narrow brick row house with three steps and a green door whose paint had blistered. They went in, and the door closed on the sound of the rain. I stood with water going down my collar and felt the loneliness that comes, absurdly, from watching other people be let into a house.

I should have gone home. Instead I crossed the street and stood beside a parked station wagon, looking through a gap in the curtains.

It was a plain room: a lamp, a sofa with a crocheted blanket, a bookcase, a small table with two chairs. The man came in without his coat and set a kettle on something out of view. The woman crossed to the window and I stepped back, but she did not look out. She slowly unbuttoned the gray coat, and beneath it she wore a dress the exact green of the chair's surviving side. Something in my chest went cold and exact.

She sat down in the armchair by the lamp. It was not the chair from the curb; this one was blue, and whole. But she sat in it the way the burned chair had sat on Delancey Street, upright, facing the road, her left side a little dimmer than her right because of how the lamplight fell. And I thought, with a certainty that embarrasses me now, that she had been the one who put it out. Or that it had been put out in her place. Some quiet trade had been made in that house, the kind a household makes with misfortune: the fire would take a chair and leave a woman.

The water had reached my ankles. It came up Marrow Street in a smooth brown sheet, without drama, carrying the sponge, which had apparently made the trip back, and a child's single red mitten. I stayed where I was. Inside, the man set a cup beside her, and she took it with her right hand, and for the first time she looked up, not at him, but past him, at the gap in the curtains, at me.

I don't say she saw me. The glass was dark on my side, and a person looking out sees only her own reflection. But she held the look for the length of a breath, and her expression was not alarmed. It was the expression of someone who has waited at a curb a long time and sees a vehicle approaching and is not certain it is the right one.

Then she lifted the cup and drank, and the man said something, and she laughed, a short, dry sound I imagined rather than heard, like a log settling in a grate.

The water was at my knees. I thought of the chair on Delancey, which by now would be lifting its good green arm in the current, its black arm trailing, turning slowly the way a thing turns when it has finally been released from the duty of staying where it was put. In the morning someone would find it against a fence and think nothing of it, and that, too, was a kind of mercy.

I went home eventually, wading, holding the pharmacy bag above my head like a man fording a river in an old painting. In my apartment I stood at the window with the lights off and kept very still, in case anyone was looking up.

The rain stopped on the twelfth day. People put their ruined furniture out on the curbs in long, sodden rows, and I walk past them each morning, looking. I tell myself I am looking for the chair. But I am looking for the woman in the gray coat, to see whether she is still sitting where she was left, or whether someone has come and lifted her gently out into the street.
